title: Inside the Halftime Music Strategy For the NFL’s International Games: ‘The Biggest Challenge Is Expectation’
summary: As the NFL expands with seven new halftime performances in seven cities around the world, the league's Tim Tubito breaks down their music strategy.
contentText:
When the NFL prepared to kick off its 2026-2027 season with an opening game in Melbourne, Australia on Sept. 10, Tim Tubito was gearing up for the beginning of his own journey of a season. The NFL’s senior director of global game presentation and entertainment, Tubito had an ambitious slate ahead of him: the league was planning its most ambitious international slate of games ever, with its largest group of major halftime headliners taking stages around the world.

So when the Jonas Brothers hit the halftime stage in Melbourne that day, it was the first of what will now become seven major halftime shows the NFL hosts in seven international cities on four different continents around the world, up from six shows in five cities last year, and marking the NFL’s major foray into this kind of event, having hosted the biggest stage in the world for decades in the annual Super Bowl Halftime Show.

“The success we had last year internationally, frankly, that was kind of a test run,” Tubito tells Billboard . “We were going to see how that was received, and it was received really well. And so, as the league expands, the idea is to continue to expand with it.”

With yesterday’s (Oct. 10) announcement that The Warning would be performing the game in Mexico City on Nov. 22, that expanded slate is now set: the Jonas Brothers played in Melbourne Sept. 10; Pedro Sampaio & Ricky Martin performed at the game in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Sept. 27; Ayra Starr headlined the game in London between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars earlier today (Oct. 11); and Burna Boy (Paris, Oct. 25), Manuel Turizo (Madrid, Nov. 8) and Cage the Elephant (Munich, Germany, Nov. 15) will round out the lineup. It’s a diverse, and global, array of stars, and helps to highlight the NFL’s further foray into the live music space, particularly as it expands around the globe.

And that expansion is not slowing down. Here, Tubito speaks about the NFL’s music strategy, the challenges and complications that can arise from hosting these types of events in venues not specially built for them, and how these performances differ from that vaunted Super Bowl stage. “Music connects to memory for people,” Tubito says. “It’s that nostalgia thing. Beyond just the halftime show itself, music plays such a big part in what we do at an NFL game.”

Sports & Music Power Players 2026 List

The NFL started doing regular season halftime shows a few years ago. Why did that first get going?

Specifically for the international games, back when we were only doing games in London, we tested out some smaller local halftime shows. And I think the expectation with international fans, especially, is they watch the Super Bowl and they expect that spectacle to be a part of it. So we started to look into growing that. And for us, there’s certainly the entertainment value in engaging the fan and creating that experience in the stadium, but it’s also a way to engage the casual fan or someone who’s not necessarily familiar with football, which is both helpful domestically but certainly helpful internationally. 

The music itself and the artists we work with reach audiences that might not necessarily be tuning into a football game, and that happens for multiple reasons and multiple touch points. So there’s the show itself, but also the lead up, whether that is on the artist channels promoting the show or artists appearing on morning news shows where football or sports aren’t typically discussed, or even publications like Billboard where it’s more of a music listener. You’re now reaching fans who might not typically be tuning into a sports network or a football game. So the idea is certainly entertainment and engaging the fans first, but it’s bringing people in who might not necessarily watch the game, and then when they tune in for the music, they stick around for the game and fall in love with the game as well.

How much have you learned from the Super Bowl Halftime Show being so successful over the years, and been able to apply that to to these kinds of shows?

The scale that we’re able to do at the Super Bowl is very different. But I think at the core, it’s the same. It starts with the artist, and it starts with developing a great idea around the artist’s music. So we work with artists that are really looking to lean in and connect with that local audience. 

Just as you saw in the Super Bowl Halftime Show this year, music is also about the storytelling behind the music. The days of, “The band just gets up on stage and plays,” that’s still great, and you love that. But having that story behind it, it brings that second layer to it, where it really connects with people a bit deeper.

Tim Tubito

Courtesy NFL

How do you choose performers?

We have a strategy behind it. It’s not just, “Let’s get the biggest name.” That’s not always the answer, especially for these international markets. We take a bunch of things into consideration: How do they resonate in the local market? And for the broadcast audience, how do they resonate globally? What kind of show do they put on? Is it a show that’s going to translate to a live audience? Because you can feel that in the broadcast if the energy in the stadium isn’t strong. So that’s a big part of it. And then their willingness to lean in with us and really create a year-round partnership, whether that’s through posting with us, attending events in the lead-up, promoting the game, promoting our causes, just being a part of things a little bit deeper.

For us, the next step has been, we get these performers, they put on a great show, we have a great experience with them, they have a great experience. We don’t want them to just leave and we never work with them again. We want that to be a kind of a year-round engagement. So that all plays a part in it, and certainly a key to it, which makes things a lot easier, is when you have artists who are authentic football fans and they care about the game as well. That really helps.

Are there particular genres that you try to go for?

It depends market by market. What resonates in Munich is certainly not the same in Mexico City, so that plays a factor in it. We’re still learning about the markets. We have great local offices who give us great intel, and we work with them. We do a lot of research on what resonates in those markets. So that’s where we start. We look at what’s resonating.

When we look at Europe or even Australia, you wouldn’t think country music, internationally, is as big as it is, but it’s tremendous. And then we’ve leaned in heavy to Latin over the past couple of years, both with halftime at the Super Bowl, but also what we did last year in some of these different markets, with Latin music exploding internationally. So I think we take those all into consideration when we go with genre. But when we do lay out the games, we do try to cross every genre. We want the music to be as diverse as our audience.

What are some of the challenges that you have in putting these together?

The biggest challenge is expectation. The expectation is Super Bowl Halftime. What we’re able to put behind all these games is not the same as Super Bowl Halftime.
